title: Microservices Decomposition Strategies
description: Learn strategies for breaking down a monolithic application into microservices using proven patterns.

data.text: Decomposing a monolith is one of the hardest tasks in software architecture. Amazon, Uber, and Spotify all used decomposition strategies to split their monoliths into manageable services. The key is to do it incrementally without disrupting users.

data.title: Proven Approaches
items: Strangler Fig: Gradually replace monolith pieces with services, letting the old system 'strangle' over time
Anti-Corruption Layer: Build an adapter layer between the monolith and new services to protect them from legacy design
Domain-Driven Design: Decompose by business capability using bounded contexts
Database per Service: Extract services with their own databases to enforce decoupling

data.text: The Strangler Fig pattern, named after the fig tree that grows around a host tree, involves placing a proxy or API gateway in front of the monolith. New functionality is built as services, while the monolith continues serving old functionality. Over time, the monolith is gradually replaced.

data.title: Real-World Example
data.text: Netflix used a similar approach when transitioning from DVD rentals to streaming. They built the new streaming service alongside the existing DVD system, routing traffic based on user type.

data.caption: Strangler Fig pattern over time
data.definition:
graph LR
    subgraph Phase1[Phase 1: Monolith + One Service]
        G1[Gateway]
        M1[Monolith]
        S1[New Service]
        G1 --> M1
        G1 -.-> S1
    end
    subgraph Phase2[Phase 2: More Services]
        G2[Gateway]
        M2[Monolith]
        S2[Service 2]
        S3[Service 3]
        G2 --> S2
        G2 --> S3
        G2 -.-> M2
    end

data.title: Example: Extracting a Payment Service
data.content: Imagine an e-commerce monolith. You first route all payment traffic to a new payment service while keeping other functionality in the monolith.
data.code:
# Step 1: Add feature flag or routing rule
# All /payments/* requests go to PaymentService
# All other requests still go to Monolith

# Step 2: Gradually shift functionality
# - Refund capability stays in monolith temporarily
# - New refund endpoints built in PaymentService
# - Monitor both systems

# Step 3: Decommission monolith payment code
# Once all payment traffic is in PaymentService,
# remove payment code from monolith

items.question: How long does decomposition take?
items.answer: It depends on the monolith size. At Amazon, it took years to fully decompose. The key is to do it incrementally without big-bang releases.

items.question: What if my team is small?
items.answer: Focus on one bounded context at a time. You do not need to extract everything at once. Start with the most painful or highest-value service.

items.question: Should I use Domain-Driven Design?
items.answer: DDD is excellent for identifying bounded contexts and service boundaries. It helps teams align on ubiquitous language and business capabilities.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Incremental decomposition reduces risk compared to big-bang rewrites
Strangler Fig is the safest starting strategy
Identify bounded contexts before extracting services
Keep the monolith running while you migrate functionality
data.takeaway: Decompose slowly and deliberately; never rewrite the entire system at once.
